`docs/QDK-Developer-Guide.md` in [qnap-dev/QDK](https://github.com/qnap-dev/QDK).

---

## QPKG-028 — Declare the web UI with the `QPKG_WEB*` and proxy fields

**What.** A package with a web UI sets `QPKG_WEBUI` (a path starting with
`/`), `QPKG_WEB_PORT`, and `QPKG_WEB_SSL_PORT` when the app serves HTTPS. To
reach it through the NAS's own port and myQNAPcloud, add
`QPKG_USE_PROXY="1"` with `QPKG_PROXY_PATH`. Keep `QPKG_DESKTOP_APP="0"`
unless the UI works inside an iframe.

**Why.** App Center builds its "Open" link from these fields; without them
the link is wrong or missing, and it shows only while the package is
enabled. `QPKG_DESKTOP_APP="1"` opens the UI in an iframe on the QTS desktop,
capped at 1178×600, which breaks apps that set `X-Frame-Options` or need
more room (QDK guide §5). Special port values: `-1` means the system web
server's port, `-2` means the protocol is not supported.

**How.**

```sh
QPKG_WEBUI="/web/"
QPKG_WEB_PORT="9101"
QPKG_WEB_SSL_PORT="-2"
QPKG_DESKTOP_APP="0"
```

**When NOT to apply.** A headless service (an S3 or API endpoint with no
UI) sets none of these.

## QPKG-029 — Set `QPKG_VOLUME_SELECT` deliberately

**What.** `qpkg.cfg` sets `QPKG_VOLUME_SELECT`: `3` lets the user choose the
install volume and migrate later, `1` allows choosing at install only, `0`
installs on the default volume without asking.

**Why.** The package directory holds everything you ship and every
hook-created data dir (QPKG-021). A large package installed on the system
volume by default can fill it, and moving it later is a manual job unless
migration was allowed (QDK guide §5). QNAP's own QuObjects uses `3`.

**How.**

```sh
QPKG_VOLUME_SELECT="3"
```

**When NOT to apply.** A tiny package with no data can keep the default.

---

## QPKG-030 — Choose default ports outside QNAP's published port list

**What.** Pick default ports that are not in
[QNAP's list of ports used by QTS, QuTS hero and QuTScloud](https://www.qnap.com/en/how-to/faq/article/what-network-ports-are-used-by-qts-quts-hero-and-qutscloud-systems),
check at `start` that the port is free, and make it configurable.

**Why.** Many upstream defaults collide on a NAS: 8080 is the NAS web UI,
8081 the Web Server, 9000 is Twonkymedia, and 8010 is QuObjects. A collision
fails at `start` with an address-in-use error, or the package answers on
the wrong service, and the user sees only a failed start (QPKG-016).

**How.**

```sh
PORT=$(/sbin/getcfg "$QPKG_NAME" Port -d 9100 -f "$QPKG_ROOT/etc/myapp.conf")
if netstat -ltn 2>/dev/null | grep -q ":$PORT "; then
    /sbin/log_tool -t2 -uSystem -p127.0.0.1 -mlocalhost -a "[$QPKG_NAME] port $PORT is in use"
    exit 1
fi
```

**When NOT to apply.** A package that replaces a QTS service on purpose and
documents that the service must be off.

## QPKG-031 — Log events with `log_tool` at the right level

**What.** User-visible events (failed start, port conflict, migration done)
go to the QTS event log with `/sbin/log_tool`, using `-t0` for information,
`-t1` for warnings and `-t2` for errors. Inside install hooks, use the QDK
helpers (`log`, `warn_log`, `err_log`).

**Why.** App Center shows only that a start failed. The event log is where a
user, and QNAP support, look first; a message only in a file under the
package directory is effectively invisible. QDK itself logs this way
(`qinstall.sh`).

**How.**

```sh
/sbin/log_tool -t1 -uSystem -p127.0.0.1 -mlocalhost -a "[$QPKG_NAME] data volume not mounted yet, retrying"
```

**When NOT to apply.** Routine per-request logging belongs in the app's own
log (QPKG-020), not the event log.

---

## QPKG-032 — Persist cron entries in `/etc/config/crontab` and reload

**What.** A package that schedules jobs appends them to
`/etc/config/crontab`, then runs
`crontab /etc/config/crontab && /etc/init.d/crond.sh restart`. It removes its
lines on uninstall (QPKG-026).

**Why.** Entries added with `crontab -e` are overwritten at the next reboot
([QNAP FAQ, How to add jobs to crontab](https://www.qnap.com/en/how-to/faq/article/how-to-add-jobs-to-crontab-to-schedule-a-job),
2024-06-25), so the job silently stops after the first restart.

**How.**

```sh
grep -q 'myapp-job' /etc/config/crontab ||
    echo "17 3 * * * $QPKG_ROOT/bin/myapp-job # myapp-job" >> /etc/config/crontab
crontab /etc/config/crontab && /etc/init.d/crond.sh restart
```

**When NOT to apply.** A long-running daemon can schedule work internally and
skip cron entirely, which leaves nothing to clean up.
